title: Addiction: Why you can't kick SYSK
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss addiction: the history of how it was viewed (from drunken colonial funerals to the 'dope fiend' character-flaw view to the current brain disease model), the dopamine reward system and how drugs hijack it, physical vs. behavioral/psychological symptoms, risk factors (genetics, peer pressure, depression, anxiety), treatment via abstinence and relapse management, US drug-use statistics for meth, prescription drugs, heroin, and cocaine, sex addiction, binge eating, gambling, alcohol, and medications used to treat addiction (Antabuse, naltrexone, nalmefene). Episode closes with an iPhone app plug and listener mail from Sarah, a thirteen-year-old fan.

entities.name: The Discovery of Addiction: Changing Conceptions of Habitual Drunkenness in America

segments.title: Opening banter and introduction to addiction
segments.summary: Hosts banter, note the episode's timing relative to the sleep episode, and introduce addiction as the topic. They discuss the Just Say No campaign's possible reverse effect on kids.

segments.title: History of how addiction was viewed
segments.summary: Harry G. Levine's history of drinking is cited, including 1678 Boston funeral and ordination drinking amounts. Views moved from substance-focused problem to character flaw ('dope fiend') to chronic disease, with opium use among middle-aged women seen as a woman's problem in the late nineteenth century.

segments.title: Dopamine, the reward system, and how drugs hijack it
segments.summary: Addiction is explained as hijacking the brain's reward system, with drugs releasing far more dopamine than natural rewards, or keeping dopamine in synapses longer. Physical dependence follows, causing withdrawal or hangover. The hosts distinguish a user from an addict.

segments.title: Symptoms of physical and behavioral addiction
segments.summary: Physical addiction shows as needing more or less of a drug, plus withdrawal symptoms like insomnia, sweating, tremors, nausea, and agitation. Behavioral or psychological symptoms include failed attempts to quit, lost jobs, and continuing despite harm.

segments.title: Brain disease model, relapse, and risk factors
segments.summary: Addiction is treated as a chronic disease with relapse and booster sessions. Risk factors include genetics, peer pressure, self-worth, anxiety, and depression. Hosts note the societal costs of addiction and argue against prohibition.

segments.title: Meth, prescription drugs, and heroin statistics
segments.summary: Meth use in the US reportedly fell by half from 2006 to 2008, and long-term meth users show damaged dopamine cells. Prescription drug abuse is rising, with a fourfold increase in rehab admissions for prescription drugs in the first decade of the century. Heroin use reportedly rose from 2007 to 2008 in past-month users, and about a quarter of people who try heroin become dependent.

segments.title: Cocaine and crack trends
segments.summary: Past-month cocaine use among kids reportedly declined from 0.6 to 0.4 percent from 2002 to 2008, and it also dropped among young adults. The hosts note these drugs target the reward center.

segments.title: Sex addiction, binge eating, and gambling
segments.summary: Sex addiction is estimated at three to six percent of Americans per NCASAC, with the hosts doubting it is overused as an excuse for celebrity misconduct. Binge eating disorder affects one to three percent of people generally and about a quarter of obese people seeking help. Gambling addiction, called ludomania, is discussed with about 2 to 15 million affected figures.

segments.title: Alcohol addiction statistics and sympathetic drug treatments
segments.summary: Alcohol is described as the biggest problem because it is legal and easily bought. Statistics include that men are three times more likely to be alcoholics, and that a happily married person has a lower chance than a single or badly married person. Medications discussed are Antabuse, which causes unpleasant reactions to drinking, and naltrexone and nalmefene, opioid antagonists. Naltrexone is reported to work for alcoholism and nalmefene for gambling.

segments.title: Genetics and epigenetics of addiction
segments.summary: Addiction is linked to gene combinations, with the ALDH2 gene making alcoholism less likely with two copies. Epigenetics is explained as how environment and drugs turn genes on and off. A variant of the opioid receptor gene is linked to lower relapse rates in alcoholism. Relapse in heroin treatment is noted as higher for the fifth time than the first.

segments.title: iPhone app promotion
segments.summary: The hosts promote the upcoming How Stuff Works iPhone app, which provides access to podcasts, videos, blogs, and articles.

segments.title: Listener mail from Sarah
segments.summary: Sarah, a thirteen-year-old listener, updates the hosts on school and asks for a podcast on theater and Dr. Seuss. She also tells a story about a cooking class mishap where cookies were made with a quarter cup of salt instead of a teaspoon.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts wrap up, invite listeners to send finger-loss stories, and give the website address for more content.
